🏠 Welcome to Lesson 1

Understanding a Short Story and the Values It Expresses

This self-learning material will guide you in reading and understanding a short story, identifying the values shown by characters, and connecting those values to your own life.

What will you learn?

You will read and understand short stories, recall important events, identify the message or value expressed, support an answer with a detail from the story, and connect that value to everyday life.

Learning competency

Analyze literary texts as expressions of individual or communal values.

Upper-Intermediate: structural context in prose and poetry, and biographical, historical, and sociocultural contexts.

Proficient: structural context in prose, poetry, and drama/film, and biographical, historical, sociocultural, and psychological contexts.

This introductory lesson uses short stories to understand how characters’ actions and story events express values. Other literary forms, elements, and contexts will be explored in succeeding lessons.

Lesson objectives

UPPER-INTERMEDIATE
  1. Recall and describe important events and details in a short story.
  2. Identify the main idea and a value expressed in the story.
  3. Select a story detail that supports the value and connect it to a familiar situation.
PROFICIENT
  1. Explain the theme or message of a short story using relevant details.
  2. Analyze how a character’s choices express an individual or communal value.
  3. Explain the relevance of that value to an individual or community experience.
Complete the activities in order. Your teacher will indicate whether you should answer the Upper-Intermediate or Proficient final assessment. Only your assigned 10-item assessment is included in your overall score.

A Helping Neighbor

One rainy afternoon, Ana saw her elderly neighbor, Lola Nena, carrying a bundle of firewood. The ground was slippery, and Lola Nena was walking slowly. Ana went over and offered to carry the bundle to the old woman’s house. Lola Nena smiled and thanked her. Ana felt happy because she had helped someone in her community.

📚 Learning content • Literary forms

What Are Literary Texts?

Definition: A literary text is a creative piece of writing that presents people, experiences, feelings, or ideas. It may express values or lessons about life.

Literary texts may take different forms. In this lesson, you will meet three common forms: prose, poetry, and drama.

📘 1. Prose – Stories in Sentences and Paragraphs

Definition: Prose is written in sentences and paragraphs. A short story is one kind of prose. It usually has characters, a setting, events, and a problem or conflict. It may express a message or value.

Example:

“Mia opened the gate. She saw her neighbor carrying a heavy basket and offered to help.”
Remember: A Helping Neighbor is a short story. It is the main text you will study in this lesson.

🎵 2. Poetry – Writing in Lines and Stanzas

Definition: Poetry is often arranged in lines and stanzas. Poets choose words carefully to express feelings, ideas, and experiences. Poems may use rhythm, rhyme, and figures of speech.

Example – Original Poem:

A helping hand,
A caring heart,
Small acts of kindness,
A brighter start.

Look for: lines, stanzas, carefully chosen words, rhythm, or rhyme.

🎭 3. Drama – A Story for Performance

Definition: Drama is written to be performed by actors. It uses dialogue (what characters say) and actions (what characters do). A play is a form of drama.

Example – Original Dialogue:

ANA: Let me carry that for you.
ALING ROSA: Thank you, Ana.
[Ana takes one side of the basket.]

Look for: character names, spoken lines, and stage directions or actions.

Important: All three—prose, poetry, and drama—are literary forms. In this lesson, you will focus on understanding a short story. You will study poetry and drama more deeply in later lessons. Drama/film is included in the Proficient-level competency; Upper-Intermediate learners may explore it for familiarization.

🔎 Quick Review: How Can You Tell Them Apart?

Literary formHow it is written or presentedWhat to look for
ProseSentences and paragraphsCharacters, setting, events, problem or conflict
PoetryLines and stanzasCarefully chosen words, feelings, rhythm, rhyme
DramaWritten for performanceDialogue, actions, characters, stage directions

E • Written response: Connect to your life

Write 3–4 sentences. Explain what you learned from Marco’s action and how you can show honesty in your family, school, or community.

Writing guide
1. I learned that honesty is important because …
2. Marco showed honesty when …
3. I can show honesty by …

Your written response is part of your Learner Activity Portfolio. Your teacher will rate it using the 5-point guide: relevant value (2), story detail (1), personal application (1), clear sentences (1).

Reflection

What? So what? Now what?

Think about Marco’s actions in “The Lost Wallet.” Use the four steps to write a reflection of 4–5 complete sentences. Explain what you learned, why it matters, and how you will use it in your own life.

1. WHAT HAPPENED?

Recall one important action in the story.

In the story, Marco …
2. SO WHAT DOES IT MEAN?

Name the value and explain what Marco’s action shows.

This shows honesty because …
3. WHY IS IT IMPORTANT?

Explain why this value matters to people.

Honesty is important because …
4. NOW WHAT WILL YOU DO?

Connect the lesson to your life and state one action you will take.

I can practice honesty by …

Model reflection

Marco returned the wallet to its owner. This showed honesty because he chose to do what was right instead of keeping something that did not belong to him. Honesty is important because it helps people trust one another. I can practice honesty by returning lost things and telling the truth.

Now write your reflection

G • Assessment

The Path We Share

Select only the level assigned by your teacher.
On Saturday, the learners of Riverside CLC planned to clean the path beside their learning center. After the rain, leaves and plastic wrappers blocked a small drainage channel. Water began to collect near the entrance. Lito wanted to leave because the work looked dirty. His classmate, Nena, reminded him that younger learners and older residents used the path every day. She put on gloves and began picking up the litter. Seeing her work, Lito joined her. Two neighbors brought sacks and a broom. They cleared the drain and placed the waste in proper containers. The path was safe again. Their teacher thanked everyone, but Nena said, “We did this together. The path belongs to all of us.” Lito realized that caring for a shared place was everyone’s responsibility.
